source_refs.note: Book p. 5: 1.3.1 Fundamental Transcendental Functions (definition with standard examples)

blocks.text: Fundamental transcendental functions are the commonly used standard transcendental functions like \(y = a^{x}\ (a > 0, a \ne 1)\), \(y = \ln x\), \(y = \sin x\), \(y = \sin^{-1} x\), which form the base for more complex transcendental functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Think of these as the "building blocks". Each belongs to a family of standard functions:

blocks.caption: Families of fundamental transcendental functions (our table)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the conditions \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\) on \(y = a^{x}\)?
If \(a = 1\), then \(1^{x} = 1\) for every \(x\): a constant function, which is algebraic, not transcendental.
If \(a < 0\), say \(a = -4\), then \((-4)^{1/2} = \sqrt{-4}\) is not a real number, so \(a^{x}\) is not defined for all real \(x\).
If \(a = 0\), then \(0^{x}\) is undefined for \(x \le 0\) (for example \(0^{-1} = \frac{1}{0}\)).
So only a positive base other than 1 gives a genuine exponential function. (This is studied in detail in 1.4.)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Fundamental transcendental functions are the standard ones: \(a^{x}\ (a > 0, a \ne 1)\), \(\ln x\), \(\sin x\), \(\sin^{-1} x\) and their families.
2. They are the base from which more complex transcendental functions are made (next subtopic).
3. In \(y = a^{x}\) the base must satisfy \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Treating \(1^{x}\) as an exponential function: it is the constant 1.
2. Writing \((-2)^{x}\) as an exponential function: it is not defined for values such as \(x = \frac{1}{2}\).
3. Thinking every function containing \(\sin\) or \(\ln\) is fundamental: \(\sin x + \ln x\) is a combination, so it is non-fundamental (see 1.3.2).
